Subject: Chaos
Note: The poem's own first metamorphosis: the proem promises to run from the first creation.

Subject: humankind
Note: Ovid gives two origins and commits to neither: the creator's seed, or fresh earth shaped by Prometheus.

Subject: Lycaön
Note: Some signs of old remain — the grey hair, the fierce eyes. The rule of Ovidian change: something is kept.

Subject: the stones
Note: On Themis' oracle. Men from the stones he threw, women from hers; the veins of rock kept their name.

Subject: the earth's seeds
Note: The second creation, after the flood. Python is born of it against the earth's will.

Subject: Daphne
Note: At her own plea. Apollo takes the tree as his emblem, so the escape becomes the god's trophy.

Subject: Io
Note: Neither punishment nor rescue: Jupiter hides his own crime from Juno by changing its victim.

Subject: Syrinx
Note: Told by Mercury to put Argus to sleep, and cut off before he reaches the ending.

Subject: the reeds
Note: A second change in the same story: bound with wax and given the maiden's name.

Subject: Argus
Note: Only the eyes change; the body stays dead on the rock.

Subject: Io
Note: Restored by degrees — horns, hooves, jaw — until whiteness was her only bovine trait.

Subject: Io
Note: Worshipped by a linened throng: Isis, though Ovid never writes the name.

Subject: the Heliads
Note: Grief works the change itself; no god is named. Their mother tears the bark and draws blood.

Subject: the Heliads
Note: Hardened by sunlight and carried down the Eridanus, someday to tempt the wives of Rome.

Subject: Cygnus
Note: For love of Phaëthon; the swan keeps to still water, mindful of Jove's bolt.

Subject: Jupiter
Note: He borrows the goddess's shape to rape her attendant; she will destroy Actaeon for seeing hers.

Subject: Callisto
Note: Punished by Juno for what Jupiter did. Her former mind remained.

Subject: Callisto and Arcas
Note: The Bears. Juno then has Ocean forbid them ever to set.

Subject: the Crow
Note: Told in flashback by the crow herself, fleeing Neptune along the shore.

Subject: Nyctimene
Note: Reported by the crow: made fowl for her foul sins, she shuns the light.

Subject: the Raven
Note: A change of colour only, for telling a truth the god did not want told.

Subject: Ocyrhoë
Note: For prophesying too much. She names her own change as it takes her voice.

Subject: Battus
Note: The touchstone, index: it still bears the informer's name.

Subject: Aglauros
Note: Not white marble — her mind had stained the stone.

Subject: Jupiter
Note: Cast off in the first line of Book 3.

Subject: Jupiter
Note: The disguise of 2.850, shed before the book gives him a name.

Subject: the dragon's teeth
Note: Sown like seed. Five survive their own civil war to found Thebes.

Subject: Actaeon
Note: Just his mind remained unchanged — he keeps it while his own hounds tear him apart.

Subject: Juno
Note: The one disguise in three books taken by a goddess, and taken to kill rather than to seduce.

Subject: Tiresias
Note: Seven years as a woman for striking two mating serpents with his staff.

Subject: Tiresias
Note: He strikes the same snakes to undo it, and so becomes the one judge who has known both sides.

Subject: Echo
Note: Her body wastes to bone, her bones to stone, and only the voice is left.

Subject: Narcissus
Note: No agent is named; the body is simply gone, the narcissus in its place.

Subject: Bacchus
Note: Fair as a girl and seemingly heavy with wine — the sailors take him for plunder.

Subject: Bacchus
Note: Grapes at his brow, a vine-wound spear, phantom tigers; the ship stops dead in the water.

Subject: Acoetes' crew
Note: Nineteen of twenty; Acoetes alone is spared, and tells it.

Subject: Dercetis
Note: Named in passing: the first tale Alcithoë's sister weighs and sets aside.

Subject: Semiramis
Note: Named in passing; her later years spent atop a tower.

Subject: a naiad, and the youths she charmed
Note: Named in passing: her herbs turned the youths to fish, then did the same to her.

Subject: the mulberry
Note: Stained by Pyramus' blood; kept dark at Thisbe's dying prayer, in mourning for the two of them.

Subject: the Sun
Note: Takes the mother's form to be let into the daughter's room.

Subject: the Sun
Note: Resumes his own light, and rapes her.

Subject: Leucothoë
Note: Buried alive by her father. The Sun rains nectar on the mound, and a sprig of incense breaks it — she reaches heaven as smoke.

Subject: Clytië
Note: Nine days on the bare ground watching him pass; rooted, pale, still turning her face after the Sun.

Subject: Daphnis
Note: Named in passing by Alcithoë.

Subject: Sithon
Note: Named in passing: “now woman, now man.”

Subject: Celmis
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: the Curetes
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: Crocus and Smilax
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: Salmacis and Hermaphroditus
Note: She prays never to be parted from him, and the prayer is granted to the letter.

Subject: the pool of Salmacis
Note: At their son's request, the pool gives his new condition to every man who bathes in it.

Subject: the looms of Minyas' daughters
Note: The weaving they did through his feast turns green.

Subject: Minyas' daughters
Note: Named for the dusk they now fly in — Latin vespertilio, from vesper.

Subject: Ino and Melicertes
Note: At Venus' plea, as they drown. Neptune changes names as well as forms.

Subject: Ino's companions
Note: For blaming Juno. Each is fixed in the gesture she was making.

Subject: Ino's companions
Note: The rest skim the water where she fell.

Subject: Cadmus
Note: He asks to become a snake if the serpent he killed was sacred — and is. The voice at 3.98 foretold it.

Subject: Harmonia
Note: She asks to follow him; mild dragons, they remember what they were.

Subject: Jupiter
Note: Named in passing: how Perseus was begotten on Danaë.

Subject: the Gorgon's blood
Note: Drops from Medusa's head over Libya — why the land teems with snakes.

Subject: Atlas
Note: For driving off a guest. Heaven and all its stars now rest on him.

Subject: the seaweed
Note: An accident of where Perseus set the head down; the sea-nymphs sow it, and coral still hardens in air.

Subject: Medusa's victims
Note: Seen by Perseus along the road to the Gorgons.

Subject: Medusa's blood
Note: Sprung from their mother's blood as her head comes off.

Subject: Medusa's hair
Note: For being raped by Neptune in Minerva's shrine. The goddess punishes the victim, and wears the snakes on her breast.

Subject: Phineus' followers
Note: For attacking the wedding feast. Thescelus mid-throw, Nileus mid-boast; two hundred in all.

Subject: Aconteus
Note: He fought on Perseus' side, and glanced once.

Subject: Phineus
Note: Promised he would last for ages; his supplicating pose is kept in marble in Cepheus' house.

Subject: Proetus
Note: For usurping Acrisius' citadel.

Subject: Polydectes
Note: For calling Medusa's death a lie.

Subject: the rock of Helicon
Note: The Hippocrene, struck by the winged horse's hoof.

Subject: the Muses
Note: They take wings to get out of Pyreneus' house; he tries to follow off the tower.

Subject: the gods
Into: ram, goat, cat, crow, cow, ibis, fish
Note: In the Pierides' song, fleeing Typhon: Jupiter a ram (why Ammon is horned), Bacchus a goat, Diana a cat, Apollo a crow, Juno a cow, Mercury an ibis, Venus a fish.

Subject: Cyane
Note: For Proserpine's rape and her own rights ignored. The thinnest parts go first — hair, fingers, feet.

Subject: Stellio
Note: For mocking her thirst. Latin stellio, a lizard flecked with star-like spots — its naming fits its shaming.

Subject: Ascalaphus
Note: For reporting the pomegranate seeds that keep her below.

Subject: the Sirens
Note: They asked for wings to search the sea for Proserpine; their faces and voices were left them.

Subject: Arethusa
Note: Hidden in a cloud from Alpheus and sweated into water, then carried under the sea to Ortygia.

Subject: Alpheus
Note: Sheds the man's shape he pursued her in, to mix his waters with hers.

Subject: Lyncus
Note: For trying to murder Triptolemus in his sleep and claim the gift of grain.

Subject: the Pierides
Note: For losing and jeering. Already magpies when Minerva meets them at 299; they keep their old prattle.

Subject: Minerva
Note: A grey wig and a cane, to warn Arachne off.

Subject: Minerva
Note: “She's come!” — and the disguise is shed.

Subject: Haemus and Rhodope
Note: Woven by Minerva in a corner of her tapestry: they called each other by the names of gods.

Subject: Oenoë
Note: Woven by Minerva: made to war on her own people.

Subject: Antigone
Note: Woven by Minerva. Laomedon's daughter, not Oedipus'.

Subject: Cinyras' daughters
Note: Woven by Minerva; a story otherwise unknown.

Subject: Jupiter
Into: bull, eagle, swan, satyr, Amphitryon, gold, flame, shepherd, snake
Note: Woven by Arachne: for Europa, Asteria, Leda, Antiope, Alcmene, Danaë, Aegina, Mnemosyne and Proserpine.

Subject: Neptune
Into: bull, Enipeus, ram, horse, winged thing, dolphin
Note: Woven by Arachne: for Canace, Iphimedia, Theophane, Ceres, Medusa and Melantho.

Subject: Apollo
Note: Woven by Arachne; the shepherd was for Isse.

Subject: Bacchus
Note: Woven by Arachne: for Erigone.

Subject: Saturn
Note: Woven by Arachne: why his son Chiron is half horse.

Subject: Arachne
Note: She has hanged herself; Minerva lets her live, and keep hanging. The drug is Hecate's.

Subject: Niobe
Note: No god touches her: grief stiffens her where she sits. A wind carries the rock to Sipylus, and it still weeps.

Subject: the Lycian peasants
Note: For fouling the water she asked to drink; still cursing in the depths.

Subject: the mourners' tears
Note: Shed for the flayed satyr, drunk by the earth and sent back up as a river bearing his name.

Subject: Pelops
Note: Reassembled after his father served him to the gods; one piece was missing.

Subject: Procne and Philomela
Note: Fleeing Tereus' sword; their breasts still carry the bloodstains.

Subject: Tereus
Note: His own pain and rage make him a bird, its beak as long as his sword.

Subject: Calaïs and Zetes
Note: Their father's wings grow in with their beards; they will sail with the Argonauts.

Subject: the dragon's teeth (Colchis)
Note: Sown by Jason, they take shape in the furrows like infants in the womb and come up already armed. A rock thrown among them sets them killing each other.

Subject: Glaucus
Note: Named in passing: Medea gathers the Anthedon grass before Glaucus has eaten it. His change is told in Book 13.

Subject: Medea's dragons
Note: The scent of the herbs alone makes them slough their aged skins, a first proof of what the brew can do.

Subject: a werewolf
Note: Named in passing among the ingredients: the entrails of a wolf that could take a man's shape.

Subject: the olive branch
Note: The dead stick she stirs with turns green, puts out leaves and bears olives: the test the brew passes before it touches Aeson.

Subject: the ground
Note: Wherever the boiling drops fall, the earth turns green.

Subject: Aeson
Note: At Jason's plea, though not on his terms. His throat is cut and refilled with the brew; his beard darkens, and he remembers being this man forty years before.

Subject: Bacchus' nurses
Note: Named in passing: Liber sees Aeson renewed and asks the same favour for the women who nursed him.

Subject: the ram
Note: A demonstration for Pelias' daughters: cut up and boiled, the ram loses its horns and its years together, and a lamb leaps from the vat.

Subject: Cerambus
Note: Named in passing on Medea's flight: lifted above Deucalion's flood on wings. The usual version makes him a beetle (commentary).

Subject: the serpent at Pitane
Note: Named in passing on Medea's flight; the commentary links it to the snake Phoebus turns to stone at 11.56–60.

Subject: the stolen calf
Note: Named in passing: on Ida, Liber hid a calf his son had stolen under a stag's false shape. The crime concealed is his son's, not his own.

Subject: Maera
Note: Named in passing; only her eerie barking is mentioned. The glossary says she became a dog.

Subject: the Coan women
Note: Named in passing: the wives of Cos grew horns as Hercules' army marched away. The story is obscure (commentary).

Subject: Ctesylla
Note: Named in passing: Alcidamas watches a dove rise from his daughter's body. The commentary names her and calls it the gods' amends for her death in childbirth.

Subject: Cygnus (son of Hyrië)
Note: Spurned by Phylius, he leaps from a cliff in a rage; all think him dead, but he rises on new white wings. Why Tempe is known for swans.

Subject: Hyrië
Note: Believing her son dead, she dissolves in tears into the lake that bears her name.

Subject: Combe
Note: Named in passing: she fled her sons on trembling wings. Nothing else is known of her (commentary).

Subject: the king and queen of Calaurea
Note: Named in passing; the story is otherwise unknown (commentary).

Subject: Cephisus' grandson
Note: Named in passing; the river-god still mourns him. Nothing else is known (commentary).

Subject: Botres
Note: Named in passing as Eumelus' winged son. The commentary supplies the story: killed by his father for impiety, he was revived by Apollo as a bird.

Subject: the mushrooms of Corinth
Note: Named in passing: in Corinth's legend the first people sprang from rain-soaked mushrooms, one more origin to set beside Book 1's.

Subject: Phene and Periphas
Note: Named in passing. The birds and the agent come from the commentary, which says Periphas had been given the honours due to Jove.

Subject: Alcyone (granddaughter of Polypemon)
Note: Named in passing. Thrown from a cliff for unchastity, she became a halcyon (commentary).

Subject: Cerberus' foam
Note: Dragged into daylight by Hercules, the hound sprays the meadows with froth, and the soil grows it into the poison Medea brews for Theseus.

Subject: Sciron's bones
Note: Refused a grave on land or at sea, the robber's bones are tossed about until they harden into the rocks that bear his name.

Subject: Arne
Note: She betrayed her island for gold, and as a black-footed jackdaw loves gold still.

Subject: the ants
Note: At Aeacus' prayer for as many subjects as the ants on Jove's oak. He dreams them shaken down and rising upright as men, wakes to find them real, and names them Myrmidons; they keep the ants' thrift.

Subject: Cephalus
Note: Dawn alters his shape so he can test Procris unrecognized: a mortal disguised by a goddess, not a god disguising himself. No change back is described; he simply declares himself (741–42).

Subject: the Teumessian fox and Hurricane
Note: Turned to marble mid-chase, so the fox that could not be caught and the hound that could not be outrun both stay unbeaten.

Subject: Jupiter
Note: Named in passing, and denied: Scylla tells Minos that no god in a bull's shape sired him, only a real bull.

Subject: Nisus
Note: Already changed when we see him, with no agent or cause given; he swoops on the daughter who stole his lock.

Subject: Scylla (daughter of Nisus)
Note: Pecked loose from Minos' stern, she hangs above the waves on new wings. The bird's name, ciris, comes from the lock she sheared.

Subject: Ariadne's crown
Note: Deserted on Naxos, Ariadne is consoled by Liber, who throws her crown into the sky. Its gems turn to fire and settle between the Kneeler and the Snake.

Subject: Daedalus and Icarus
Note: Barred from land and sea by Minos, Daedalus “altered nature” with feathers, thread and wax. Watching peasants take the fliers for gods.

Subject: Icarus (son of Daedalus)
Note: He flies too near the sun; the wax softens, the feathers go, and his bare arms beat the air as he falls into the sea that takes his name.

Subject: Perdix
Note: Thrown from the Acropolis by his jealous uncle, he is caught by Minerva, who loves a clever mind, and feathered in midair. His name survives the change, and the bird still keeps low for fear of falling.

Subject: Caeneus
Note: Named in passing in the hunters' catalogue: “no maid now.” The story waits for 12.189ff.

Subject: Castor and Pollux
Note: Named in passing, as a change still to come: “not yet two stars in heaven.”

Subject: Meleäger's sisters
Note: Diana, sated at last with the ruin of Oeneus' house, gives the mourning sisters wings and beaks, all but Gorge and Deianira. The commentary names the birds meleagrides, guineafowl.

Subject: the Echinades
Note: They sacrificed to every local god but him. In flood he tears them away with the ground they stood on, and the sea splits it into five islands.

Subject: Perimele
Note: Thrown into the sea by her father after Acheloüs raped her; at the river's plea Neptune turns her swimming body to land, and the island keeps her name.

Subject: Jupiter and Mercury
Note: Jupiter in mortal guise, Mercury without his wand and wings. They declare themselves at 689; no change back is described.

Subject: the neighbours' land
Note: For the thousand doors shut against the gods; everything but the old couple's house sinks into marsh.

Subject: Baucis and Philemon's hut
Note: Posts become columns, the thatch turns gold, the doors are carved and the floor paved with marble.

Subject: Baucis and Philemon
Note: Granted their wish to die in the same hour: each sees the other sprout leaves, and they say farewell as the bark closes over their mouths.

Subject: Proteus
Into: lion, youth, boar, snake, bull, stone, tree, stream, flame
Note: Acheloüs' example of a god who passes through many forms instead of keeping one.

Subject: Mestra
Note: Sold by her father, she begs Neptune, who once raped her, to steal her from her master. He gives her a fisherman's shape, and her pursuer asks the fisherman where the girl went.

Subject: Mestra
Note: Once her baffled master has gone, she changes back.

Subject: Mestra
Note: Her father, seeing she can change, sells her again and again; each time she slips away in a new shape to pay for his eating.

Subject: Acheloüs
Note: His own, narrower range of forms. The horn he has lost is Book 9's story.

Subject: Acheloüs
Note: Beaten as a wrestler, he slips out as a snake; Hercules, who strangled snakes in his cradle, mocks the borrowed shape.

Subject: Acheloüs
Note: His third and last form. Hercules drives the horns into the sand and tears one off.

Subject: Acheloüs' horn
Note: Filled by the Naiads with flowers and fruit; a nymph serves the guests from it at 89–92.

Subject: Lichas
Note: Hurled out to sea for a gift he never knew was poison. Fear drains his blood in mid-air, as cold turns rain to hail; the rock off Euboea still bears his name.

Subject: Hercules
Note: The fire takes only what came from his mother; the rest sheds it like a snake its skin and rides to the stars, heavy enough for Atlas to feel.

Subject: Galanthis
Note: For the lie that broke the spell on Alcmene's labour. She keeps her colouring and her bustle, and since her mouth lied to bring a birth, she gives birth through it.

Subject: Lotus
Note: Named in passing by Iole: she fled Priapus' assault, and the plant that bears her name bleeds when picked.

Subject: Dryope
Note: Her only fault is picking the lotus's flowers unawares, and no god is named. Soucy makes her an oak where the manuscripts say lotus; her face goes last.

Subject: Iolaüs
Note: Made young again by the goddess of youth, at the wish of her new husband, Hercules.

Subject: Callirhoë's sons
Note: Foretold by Themis: Jove will grow them up at their mother's plea, so they can avenge their father.

Subject: Byblis
Note: She weeps into the leaves until she is all tears; the Naiads make of them a spring that cannot dry, under a holly tree.

Subject: Iphis (child of Ligdus)
Note: Telethusa's prayer, the day before the wedding. The change is watched as it happens, from the longer stride to the shorter hair, and recorded on a plaque.

Subject: the man who saw Cerberus
Note: Named in passing, in a simile for Orpheus' shock: he saw Cerberus in chains and fright alone turned him to stone; no cause is given.

Subject: Olenus and Lethaea
Note: Named in passing: she boasted of her beauty, and he took her guilt on himself to share her fate on Ida.

Subject: Attis
Note: Named in passing among the trees that gather to Orpheus' song: Cybele's consort put his manhood by and stiffened into a pine.

Subject: Cyparissus
Note: He asks heaven to let him mourn forever; his tears drain his blood, and he greens and stiffens into the tree mourners plant.

Subject: Jupiter
Note: For Ganymede: the only bird he thought worthy was the one that carries his bolts.

Subject: Ganymede
Note: Carried to Olympus, where he still pours Jove's nectar, to Juno's lasting spite; Soucy's note says he was made immortal.

Subject: Ajax (son of Telamon)
Note: Foretold by Apollo in bracketed lines: Ajax's blood will one day make the same flower (13.394ff).

Subject: Hyacinth's blood
Note: Only the blood changes: a flower shaped like a lily but purple, which Apollo marks with his own lament, AI AI.

Subject: the Cerastae
Note: For killing guests at the altar of Jove of guests. Weighing exile against death, Venus takes the middle way and keeps their horns.

Subject: the Propoetides
Note: For denying her godhead Venus makes them the first prostitutes; past blushing, their blood hardens and they turn to stone, scarcely changed.

Subject: Pygmalion's statue
Note: He prays for a wife “like my ivory maid”; the ivory softens under his touch like wax in the sun, and her first sight is her lover and the sky.

Subject: Icarus and Erigone
Note: Named in passing as stars of filial devotion that hide their faces from Myrrha's crime; Soucy's note says both were set in the sky for Erigone's grief.

Subject: Myrrha
Note: She begs to be shut out from the living and the dead alike, and “her prayers found gods.” Her tears are the resin, which still bears her name.

Subject: Hippomenes and Atalanta
Note: Venus' revenge for his ingratitude: she fills him with lust in Cybele's shrine, and the goddess makes them lions to draw her chariot.

Subject: Adonis' blood
Note: Venus sprinkles nectar on the blood, and within an hour a blood-red flower springs up, as short-lived as he was and shaken off by the wind it is named for.

Subject: Minthe
Note: Named in passing by Venus, as precedent for her own right to change Adonis; the text gives no cause, and Soucy's note says Minthe tried to seduce Dis.

Subject: the snake at Methymna
Note: It strikes at Orpheus' severed head on the beach and is fixed with its jaws still open; Medea flies past it at 7.357–58.

Subject: the Ciconian women
Note: Rooted where each stood in the chase; reaching to beat her thighs in grief, each strikes oak.

Subject: what Midas touches
From: twig, stone, earth, grain, water, food, wine
Note: His own wish, granted to the letter: bread and meat harden at his lips, and wine runs gold between his teeth.

Subject: Midas
Note: At his plea, Bacchus sends him to bathe at the source of the river by Sardis; the gilding leaves his body for the stream.

Subject: the Pactolus
Note: The power Midas washes off passes into the water, and its fields are still hard with gold: Ovid's account of the Pactolus' gold.

Subject: Midas' ears
Note: For preferring Pan's pipes to the lyre. Only the offending part changes, and he hides it under a purple hood.

Subject: the barber's whisper
Note: Midas' barber breathes the secret into a pit; the reeds that spring there repeat it in the south wind.

Subject: Apollo
Note: To build Troy's walls for Laömedon alongside Neptune; the king then refuses the promised pay. The god's return to his own form is not told.

Subject: the land of Troy
Note: For Laömedon's broken bargain over the walls. The crops drown, and the king's daughter is owed to a sea-monster.

Subject: Thetis
Note: Her usual defence against Peleus' assault in the grotto; the tigress makes him let go.

Subject: Thetis
Note: Chained in her sleep on Proteus' advice, she begins to change, finds herself held, and yields; Achilles is conceived.

Subject: Apollo
Note: He comes to Chione by night, after Mercury has raped her by day; she bears a son to each.

Subject: Daedalion
Note: Caught in mid-leap from Parnassus, mad with grief for his daughter. He keeps his old ferocity and now preys on other birds.

Subject: the wolf of Psamathe
Note: Peleus prays and Thetis pleads, and Psamathe relents; the wolf turns to stone mid-kill, unchanged but for its colour.

Subject: the sons of Sleep
Into: people; beasts, birds, snakes; clods, stones, waves, trees
Note: Named in passing, as their trades: Morpheus plays people, Likeness animals, Phantasm lifeless things.

Subject: Morpheus
Note: Sent by Sleep at Juno's bidding, he sheds his wings at Trachis and stands by Alcyone's bed pale, naked and dripping: a false shape with a true report.

Subject: Ceÿx and Alcyone
Note: She leaps from the breakwater already winged; the gods change her drowned husband too. The seven calm days of winter when the halcyon nests are theirs.

Subject: Aesacus
Note: Tethys feathers him as he leaps and will not let him drown. He keeps diving, and the habit names him: Latin mergus, “diver.”

Subject: the serpent at Aulis
Note: An omen, as in Homer: having eaten the eight chicks and their mother, it is left in stone round the plane-tree, and Calchas reads nine years of war.

Subject: Cygnus (son of Neptune)
Note: Strangled by Achilles with his own chinstrap; the armour is found empty. The third Cygnus to become the bird of his name, and the cause of Achilles' death (580–83).

Subject: Caenis
Note: Her wish after Neptune rapes her: never to suffer it again. He adds a body no blade can wound, and she ends the request in a man's voice.

Subject: Caeneus
Note: Smothered under the forests the centaurs heap on him. Nestor gives both versions: the underworld, or a unique gold-winged bird, seen by Nestor too, that Mopsus hails as Caeneus.

Subject: Periclymenus
Note: A power from his grandfather Neptune. As Jupiter's eagle he claws Hercules' face and is shot down from the clouds.

Subject: Ajax's blood
Note: His blood forces out the sword, and the ground puts forth the flower that once grew from Hyacinth; its letters, AI AI, now read as his name as well as a cry of grief.

Subject: Hyacinth
Note: Named in passing: the flower Ajax's blood brings back first sprang from the Spartan boy (Book 10).

Subject: Hecuba
Note: Stoned by the Thracians after she blinds Polymestor, she meets the rocks with growls and bites, and her words come out as barks; the place is named for it. Even Juno says she had not deserved it.

Subject: Memnon's ashes
Note: Granted when Dawn asks only for some honour for her son. The pyre's smoke congeals into birds that split into two camps and fight to the death over his ashes, every year.

Subject: whatever Anius' daughters touched
Note: A power from Liber “beyond belief or prayer” — and the reason Agamemnon seizes the girls to feed his fleet.

Subject: Anius' daughters
Note: They call on Bacchus as Agamemnon's men come with chains. Anius never learned how it happened, and doubts that being destroyed counts as help. White doves are Venus' birds.

Subject: Orion's daughters' ashes
Note: Engraved on Alcon's bowl: the two maidens die for Thebes, and their dust brings forth sons so that their line will not end.

Subject: Cragaleus
Note: Named in passing, and not by name; Soucy's note supplies the story — he awarded Ambracia to Hercules instead of Apollo.

Subject: Munichus' sons
Note: Named in passing: the Molossian king's sons take wing to escape a fire set by bandits (Soucy's note).

Subject: Scylla (the monster)
Note: Anticipated in passing: her face is still a girl's, “if bards are ever truthful.” The change itself waits for Book 14.

Subject: Acis' blood
Note: Running from under the rock that crushed him, the red fades to the colour of a flooded stream and then runs clear.

Subject: Acis
Note: “We” give him back his grandfather's powers: he stands waist-deep in the split rock, larger, sea-green and horned, the god of the river that bears his name.

Subject: Glaucus
Agent: Tethys and Ocean, at the sea-gods' asking
Note: He chews the grass that revived his catch and leaps into the sea. Judged worthy, he is purged with nine chants and a hundred rivers, and wakes green-bearded and fish-tailed, his mind changed too.

Subject: Glaucus
Note: Named in passing: he credits herbs with his own change, told at the end of Book 13.

Subject: Scylla (the monster)
Note: Circe cannot harm the man she loves, so she poisons the pool of the girl he prefers. Scylla slaps at the dogs before she sees they are part of her.

Subject: Scylla (the monster)
Note: Turned to stone before she could wreck the Trojan fleet; the rock still stands in the strait, and sailors still steer clear of it.

Subject: the Cercopes
Note: For their tricks and perjuries: limbs shrunk, noses snubbed, faces furrowed, speech cut to screeches. Their island, Pithecusae, is named for them.

Subject: the Sibyl
Note: Foretold by herself, in lines Tarrant brackets. She asked Apollo for as many years as grains of sand, not for youth, and will shrink until only her voice is left, like Echo.

Subject: Ulysses' crew
Note: No offence is named: a drugged cup and a stroke of the wand. Macar describes his own bristles, grunts and snout; Eurylochus refused the cup and stayed a man.

Subject: Ulysses' crew
Note: Ulysses' wedding-price: counter-spells and a back-turned wand, and the men rise from the sty weeping.

Subject: Picus
Note: For refusing her. His purple cloak colours the plumes and his gold clasp rings his neck; only his name is left, and it means woodpecker.

Subject: Picus' men
Note: They threaten her with spears; one touch of the wand, and not one of them keeps his shape.

Subject: Canens
Note: Six days' wandering, then she wastes away on the Tiber's bank with a dying swan's song. A spot the Camenae named for her keeps her memory.

Subject: Acmon
Note: For scorning Venus' anger: his voice thins, plumes clothe him, his arms bend into wings, and his face hardens into a beak.

Subject: Diomedes' crew
Note: Rhexenor, Lycus, Idas, Nycteus and Abas change as they stare, though most of the crew had rebuked Acmon. White and swan-like, but not swans.

Subject: the Apulian shepherd
Note: For mocking the nymphs' dance with vulgar jeers. Bark shuts his mouth, and the berries keep his tongue's bitterness.

Subject: Aeneas' ships
Note: Cybele saves the pines of her Ida from Turnus' fire: planks to flesh, sterns to heads, oars to legs, keel to spine, still sea-green. They help sailors ever after, unless the sailors are Greek.

Subject: Alcinoüs' ship
Note: Named in passing: the Phaeacian ship that brought Ulysses home, its timbers petrified, to the sea-nymphs' delight.

Subject: Ardea
Note: A city, not a person: the heron (Latin ardea) rises from the ashes, gaunt and pale, and mourns its own town.

Subject: Aeneas
Note: At Venus' plea, with Jupiter's consent. The Numicius washes away all of him that could die; she anoints him, and Rome worships him as Indiges.

Subject: Vertumnus
Note: In peasant rags with gifts of grain — the first of the guises that win him a look at Pomona.

Subject: Vertumnus
Note: Wreathed in fresh-mown grass, as if just in from tossing hay.

Subject: Vertumnus
Note: Goad in hand, as though he had just unyoked his team.

Subject: Vertumnus
Note: With a hook for pruning vines and trimming shoots.

Subject: Vertumnus
Note: With a ladder, as though come to pick fruit.

Subject: Vertumnus
Note: With a sword. This guise and the next share a line Tarrant brackets as doubtful.

Subject: Vertumnus
Note: With a rod, in the same bracketed line.

Subject: Vertumnus
Note: Grey hair, a painted headscarf, and kisses no real old woman would give. In this shape he pleads his own suit and tells the tale of Iphis.

Subject: Anaxarete
Note: The vengeful god, presumably Love, works as she looks down at Iphis' corpse: her eyes harden and the stone in her heart spreads through her limbs. Her statue stands at Salamis.

Subject: Vertumnus
Note: He sheds the guise of age and shines like the sun through cloud. He would have used force; he did not need to.

Subject: the spring by Janus' temple
Note: At Venus' request the nymphs stoke its veins with sulphur and pitch, and the gate Juno opened to the Sabines is barred by fire.

Subject: Romulus
Note: Mars claims Jupiter's promise. Snatched into his chariot, Romulus' flesh melts away like a sling's lead shot, and he appears in fairer form as Quirinus.

Subject: Hersilie
Note: Juno sends Iris to fetch her; a falling star sets her hair alight, she vanishes with it, and Romulus names her Hora.

Subject: Hercules
Note: Named in passing: Myscelus' prayer recalls the twelve Labors that won him heaven.

Subject: the pebbles in the urn
Note: Condemned for obeying the god, Myscelus prays to Hercules; every black stone in the urn comes out white.

Subject: Pythagoras
Note: The first change in his catalogue is his own soul's: he knew Euphorbus' shield when he saw it in Juno's temple at Argos.

Subject: the soul
Note: Like wax, it takes new shapes and stays itself — the ground of his ban on eating meat.

Subject: night
Note: Day follows night, and the sky changes colour from midnight to dawn.

Subject: the sun's disc
Into: white at noon, red at setting
Note: Red where the air is thick near the earth, white at its height where the air is purer.

Subject: the moon
Note: Named in passing: Diana's orb is never the same two nights running.

Subject: the year
Note: Four seasons as four ages: tender child, lusty youth, greying maturity, balding old age.

Subject: the human body
Note: Nature frees the seed into the air; it crawls, stands, grows strong, and slides into decline.

Subject: Milo
Note: Named in passing: the wrestler weeps at arms that once bulged like Hercules' and now hang slack.

Subject: Helen
Note: Named in passing: wrinkled in her mirror, she wonders why she was ever stolen twice.

Subject: the elements
Note: Earth thins to water, water to air, air to fire; then fire thickens back down the same chain.

Subject: the Ages
Note: Named in passing: Book 1's descent of the ages, now offered as proof that nothing keeps one look for long.

Subject: dry land
Note: Named in passing: he has seen it with his own eyes.

Subject: the sea
Note: Named in passing: the proof is anchors found on mountaintops and seashells far from any shore.

Subject: plains
Note: Named in passing: cut by falling water.

Subject: mountains
Note: Named in passing: washed out to sea by floods.

Subject: swamps
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: sands
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: springs and rivers
Note: Named in passing: Nature opens springs and seals them, and earthquakes send rivers gushing up or out of sight.

Subject: the Lycus
Note: Named in passing: swallowed by a gorge, it rises again from new springs far away.

Subject: the Erasinus
Note: Named in passing: it runs underground and comes up again in Argos.

Subject: the Mysus
Note: Named in passing: ashamed of its headwaters, it flows on under another name.

Subject: the Amenanus
Note: Named in passing: a Sicilian river, now running, now dry at its source.

Subject: the Anigrus
Note: Named in passing: the centaurs washed the wounds of Hercules' arrows in it, if the poets are to be believed.

Subject: the Hypanis
Note: Named in passing: sweet from the Scythian hills, bitter further down.

Subject: Antissa, Pharos and Tyre
Note: Named in passing: once ringed by sea, now joined to the shore. Soucy notes that only Antissa could have changed naturally; the others got causeways from Alexander.

Subject: Leucas
Note: Named in passing: once a headland, now standing in the open sea.

Subject: Zancle
Note: Named in passing: Sicily, cut off as the waters wore the straits away.

Subject: Helice and Buris
Note: Named in passing: sailors still point out their walls beneath the waves.

Subject: a plain near Troezen
Note: Winds shut underground swelled the earth like a blown-up bladder, and the swelling hardened with age.

Subject: the spring of Ammon
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: the Athamanes' water
Note: Named in passing: poured under a crescent moon, it sets wood alight.

Subject: what the Cicones' streams touch
Note: Named in passing: their water makes marble and turns drinkers' guts to stone.

Subject: hair washed in the Sybaris and Crathis
Note: Named in passing: two rivers on Croton's own coast.

Subject: bathers in Salmacis' pool
Note: Named in passing: the pool of 4.385–88, now listed among waters that change the mind as well as the body.

Subject: drinkers at the Aethiopian lakes
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: drinkers at Clitor's spring
Note: Either the water resists wine's warmth, or Melampus drained his purging drugs there after curing Proetus' daughters.

Subject: drinkers at the Lyncus
Note: Named in passing: the opposite of Clitor's spring.

Subject: the water at Pheneus
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: Ortygia
Note: Named in passing: Delos, once adrift, now stands still.

Subject: the Symplegades
Note: Named in passing: the Clashing Rocks that frightened the Argo now hold firm in the wind.

Subject: Aetna
Note: Its fires have not always burned and will not always: they starve when the earth stops feeding them.

Subject: the Hyperboreans
Note: Named in passing: after nine baths in Triton's marsh, so it is said; Pythagoras does not believe it.

Subject: the Scythian women
Note: Named in passing: said to manage the same with magic balms.

Subject: a rotting corpse
Note: The first of his spontaneous generations, offered as tested truth: heat and time do the work.

Subject: slaughtered bulls
Note: Bugonia, a common belief that Virgil also describes; the bees toil as their parents did.

Subject: warhorses
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: a shore crab
Note: Named in passing: planted in the ground, it rises with its tail poised to strike.

Subject: larvae
Note: Named in passing: true, unlike most of its neighbours on the list; butterflies were carved on tombs for the soul.

Subject: frogs
Note: Footless first, then swimming legs, then legs for leaping.

Subject: a bear cub
Note: Named in passing: licked into shape by its mother's tongue.

Subject: honeybees
Note: Named in passing: born in the wax hexagons; legs come late and wings later still.

Subject: birds
Note: Named in passing: the peacock, the eagle, Venus' doves — no one would believe it who had not seen it.

Subject: human marrow
Note: Named in passing: some think so; he only reports it.

Subject: the phoenix
Note: The one creature that renews itself: after five centuries it dies in a nest of spices, and the young bird carries the nest to Hyperion's shrine at Heliopolis.

Subject: the hyena
Note: Named in passing.

Subject: the chameleon
Note: Named in passing: fed on wind and air, and never named.

Subject: lynxes' urine
Note: Named in passing: from the lynxes Bacchus won in India.

Subject: coral
Note: Named in passing: compare the seaweed hardened by Medusa's head at 4.744–52.

Subject: Troy
Note: Nations rise and fall: ten years of war, and nothing left but rubble.

Subject: Rome
Note: Rumoured and prophesied — “she'll change through growth.” Growth, too, is change.

Subject: Iulus' heir
Note: Foretold by Helenus to Aeneas, as Pythagoras, once a Trojan, remembers; probably Augustus.

Subject: Hippolytus
Note: Torn apart by his own horses, he is healed with Paean's herbs, to Dis' dismay.

Subject: Hippolytus
Note: To hide his return from the dead, Diana wraps him in cloud and ages his face past recognition.

Subject: Hippolytus
Note: Renamed “twice a man” and set in her grove at Aricia; his old name smacked of horses.

Subject: Egeria
Note: Dissolved in tears for Numa; Phoebe makes her corpse a spring of “everlasting waves” — permanence, against Pythagoras' rule of flux.

Subject: Tages
Note: A clod in an Etruscan field moves, sheds its soil, and speaks of things to come.

Subject: Romulus' spear
Note: Planted on the Palatine, it puts out leaves and roots: a weapon no more.

Subject: Cipus
Note: A portent, not a punishment: the seer reads the horns as kingship, and Cipus chooses exile over the crown.

Subject: Asclepius
Note: Promised in the envoy's dream — the snake of his staff, only larger. In this shape he sails to Rome.

Subject: Asclepius
Note: On the Tiber Island he leaves the ship and takes the healer's features again, and the plague ends.

Subject: the Morning Star and the Moon
Note: Among the omens before Caesar's murder, with rains of gore and weeping statues.

Subject: Augustus Caesar
Note: Foretold by Jupiter, not before he reaches Nestor's age; the poet prays the day may come late.

Subject: Julius Caesar
Note: Venus catches the soul as it leaves the corpse; it kindles in her arms, and she lets it rise past the moon trailing its flaming tail.

Subject: Ovid
Note: The last metamorphosis: his better part borne past the stars, alive wherever he is read.
